Every piece of analysis follows the same path, whether it takes two hours or six months. This
section sets out that path, who is involved at each point, and what assurance happens along the way.

The single most important thing to take from it is that **assurance happens throughout, not at the
end**. Checking work only once it is finished tells you whether it is wrong. It does not stop it
being wrong, and by then the time to do anything about it has usually gone.

## The four phases

The lifecycle has four phases, following the AQuA Book.

::: {.callout-note title="The four phases" appearance="minimal" icon=false}
<br>
**1. Engagement and scoping.** Agreeing what question is being answered, why, and how much
assurance the answer needs.

**2. Design.** Deciding how it will be answered, and planning the assurance the level calls for.

**3. Analysis.** Doing the work, and checking it as you go.

**4. Delivery and sign-off.** Communicating the result honestly, and approving it.

**Then: review.** What happened to the analysis after it was released, and what the next piece of
work should do differently. This is a stage in its own right, it repeats, and it is
[section 11](../11-review-and-continuous-improvement/index.qmd).
:::

{{< include /guidance/_partials/diagram-lifecycle.qmd >}}

The four phases describe producing an analysis, which is where the AQuA Book's lifecycle ends.
Review sits after them because it is about the released output rather than the work, and it happens
more than once. What happens to an analysis after it is released is GovS 010's own subject at
sections 6.10, learning from experience, and 6.13, monitoring and evaluation after implementation;
it is the Code of Practice's Value pillar for anything published; and it is the Magenta Book's whole
subject where the analysis supported an intervention.

Phases are not a one-way street. Scoping, design and analysis are frequently revisited as you learn
more, and that is normal rather than a sign something has gone wrong. What should not change late
without a recorded reason is the assurance level, because that is the judgement everything else
rests on.

## Phase 1: engagement and scoping

The commissioner and the analyst agree what is actually being asked.

**You should record the purpose of the analysis and the level of quality and certainty needed to
achieve it.**[^src-govs-010-section-5-2] This is not bureaucracy. It is the only thing that later tells
anyone whether the analysis did what it was asked to do.

Explore the boundaries and scope with stakeholders, and seek a wide range of perspectives before
settling the question.[^src-govs-010-section-5-2]

If a request arrives already framed as an output rather than a question, say so and reframe it.
Providing appropriate challenge is expected of you, not obstructive, and GovS 010 section 6.2 is
explicit that analysts partner with policy colleagues and provide challenge where appropriate. The
record of that conversation is what makes the challenge defensible afterwards.

### Is it Business Critical?

{{< include /guidance/_partials/bca-determination.qmd >}}

{{< include /guidance/_partials/diagram-bca-route.qmd >}}

Everything that follows from a yes is gathered in
[section 8, Business Critical analysis](/guidance/08-business-critical/index.qmd).

### Setting the assurance level

How much assurance a piece of work needs depends on its risk, complexity and impact.[^src-govs-010-section-6-8] That is decided here, at scoping, and not later.

The specification you agree with your commissioner is where the level of assurance required is
defined, and it should state the acceptable level of risk alongside it.[^src-aqua-book-section-6-1-2]
GovS 010 asks for the levels of quality and certainty required to be recorded at the same point.[^src-govs-010-section-5-2] The Business Critical answer above feeds straight into it.

[Section 5, deciding your assurance level](../05-deciding-your-assurance-level/index.qmd), sets out
how to reach that decision and record it. It takes about five minutes.

::: {.callout-important title="Early enough to change the method" appearance="minimal" icon=false}
<br>
A level chosen before the work starts is a judgement about the work. One chosen afterwards is a
description of what happened to be done. Only the first is assurance.

It also has to be early enough to shape the design rather than describe it. A level agreed once the
method is already chosen cannot change the method.

If circumstances genuinely change, change the level and record why. Reuse is the most common
legitimate reason: analysis built once and then run monthly is a different piece of work.
:::

**What good looks like at this phase:** the commissioner can state the decision the analysis
supports, the analyst can state the question in one sentence, the Business Critical answer is
recorded either way, and the assurance level is agreed and written down. If any of the four is
missing, you are not ready to move on.

## Phase 2: design

This is where the assurance the level calls for is turned into a plan, and it is the phase that
decides how much of the rest will have to be done twice. The level itself came out of scoping.

Produce a design and plan covering the analytical cycle, and share it with everyone involved.[^src-govs-010-section-5-3] It should cover the data to be used, the method, how uncertainty will be
identified and communicated, the assumptions and known limitations, ethical and information
governance considerations, the outputs, timescales and resources, and the assurance activities
themselves.

Your design should:[^src-govs-010-section-5-3]

- **be repeatable**, producing the same results from the same inputs if someone else runs it
- consider uncertainty
- consider whether the underlying data sources are fit to answer the question
- be documented

### Planning the assurance the level requires

The level came from scoping. What happens here is turning it into something that will actually be
done. Establish the assurance requirements, develop a plan for proportionate verification and
validation, and **plan in sufficient time for the assurance activity**.[^src-aqua-book-section-7-1-2]
Your assurer should review that plan, confirm they can carry out the assurance it asks for, and
plan their own time for it.[^src-aqua-book-section-7-1-3]

The last of those is the one most often skipped. An assurance plan with no time in the schedule is
a statement of intent, not a plan.

[Section 6, doing the work](../06-doing-the-work/index.qmd), sets out what each level requires.

### The design gate

A critical friend or analytical assurer confirms that the approach meets the commissioner's needs
and answers the question, and that the assurance planned is at the right level. The commissioner
approves the design before work proceeds.[^src-govs-010-section-5-3]

Name your reviewer before the work starts, not after it finishes. A reviewer found afterwards
reviews what was produced. A reviewer named beforehand shapes what gets produced, which is
considerably more useful and usually cheaper.

## Phase 3: analysis

Undertake the analysis following the approved design and plan.[^src-govs-010-section-5-4]

Quality assurance runs through this phase rather than sitting at the end of it. Verification asks
whether the analysis was conducted properly. Validation asks whether the right kind of analysis was
used at all. Both should be proportionate to the purpose and constraints of the work, and both
should happen throughout the cycle.[^src-govs-010-section-6-6]

**Document the verification and validation activities you carry out, and what you concluded from
them.**[^src-govs-010-section-6-6] This is what a quality assurance log is for. A checklist shows
somebody knew what to do. A log shows they did it, when, and what they found.

Keep records proportionate to the work. They can include the specification and design, **notes of
any deviations from the plan**, a log of data and assumptions, an outline of the assurance
activities, technical documentation, and **lessons learned**. Records should be version controlled,
securely stored and retrievable.[^src-govs-010-section-6-7]

::: {.callout-note title="Lessons are captured as you go" appearance="minimal" icon=false}
<br>
Identify relevant lessons from earlier work when you plan, and capture new ones throughout rather
than reconstructing them at the end.[^src-govs-010-sections-6-7-and-6-10]

Lessons written up a month later are a summary of what someone remembers. Lessons written down when
they happen are evidence.
:::

Where your analysis involves code, the
[NHSBSA Analytical Code Assurance Playbook](https://nhsbsa-data-analytics.github.io/nhsbsa-analytical-code-assurance-playbook)
sets out expectations for version control, testing, peer review and documentation.

## Phase 4: delivery and sign-off

Deliver draft results to the commissioner so they are properly understood before anything is
approved.[^src-govs-010-section-5-5]

**What you deliver includes an assurance statement.** That statement covers the assumptions made,
the uncertainty, the limitations, and what the results can and cannot be used for, together with
links to references, code and data.

GovS 010 section 5.5 puts this as a should. This playbook requires it at every assurance level,
because a result whose assumptions travel separately from it is a result that will be used without
them.

[Section 9, communicating analysis](../09-communicating-analysis/index.qmd), shows what a good assurance statement looks like and gives
a worked example.

Communicate findings, limitations and uncertainty clearly, objectively and impartially.[^src-govs-010-section-6-4] Where you can express uncertainty quantitatively, do so, and avoid
unwarranted confidence in any single option.[^src-govs-010-section-6-5]

::: {.callout-important title="Caveats travel with the number, or they do not travel" appearance="minimal" icon=false}
<br>
State a material caveat in the same place as the figure it qualifies, not in an annex. Figures get
copied into slides and papers; annexes do not follow them.

If a caveat is too long to sit alongside the number, the number is not yet ready to be quoted.
:::

Sign-off then approves the analytical results.[^src-govs-010-section-5-6] Who signs off depends on the
assurance level, and [section 6, doing the work](../06-doing-the-work/index.qmd), sets that out per level.

## Assurance activity at every phase

| Phase | Assurance activity | Who |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Engagement and scoping | Purpose, and the quality and certainty required, recorded. Assurance level agreed and recorded | Commissioner and analyst |
| 2. Design | The assurance the level requires turned into a plan, with time in the schedule. Design confirmed as fit for purpose | Analyst, critical friend, commissioner |
| 3. Analysis | Verification and validation throughout, documented with conclusions | Analyst and critical friend |
| 4. Delivery and sign-off | Assurance statement produced. Results approved | Analyst, commissioner, approver |

Notice that no row is empty. That is the point of the table.

## How this maps to other structures

You may meet the analytical lifecycle described with different names elsewhere. They describe the
same path.

| This playbook, and the AQuA Book | GovS 010 | Other names you may meet |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Engagement and scoping | 5.2 Initial customer engagement and scoping | Customer engagement |
| 2. Design | 5.3 Designing the analysis | Analysis design |
| 3. Analysis | 5.4 Conducting and checking analysis | Conducting the analysis |
| 4. Delivery and sign-off | 5.5 Delivering the analysis, 5.6 Sign-off | Delivery and approval, Approval and distribution |
| **5. Review**, [section 11](../11-review-and-continuous-improvement/index.qmd) | 6.10 Learning from experience, 6.13 Monitoring and evaluation after implementation | Review |

**Delivery and sign-off is one phase, not two.** Some documents split approval from distribution.
GovS 010 keeps them adjacent at sections 5.5 and 5.6 and the AQuA Book treats them as one stage, so
this playbook does too. Carrying approval in two names leaves a reader with two places to look for
the same obligation.
